Attribution-guided distillation identifies core latents that remain systematically useful for reconstruction, unlike a randomly initialized core which is driven towards zero activity.
papers.limitation:
Requires multiple cycles of distillation, leading to much higher computational costs relative to training a single Matryoshka SAE.
Core selection depends on the gradient × activation attribution method, which is a fast first-order approximation but may be suboptimal.
Freezing encoder weight vectors stabilizes detection directions, but encoder biases and decoder weights are reinitialized, so latent behavior (threshold, firing rate, contribution) can still change across cycles.
future_direction: Reducing the computational cost of distillation.
Extending the DMSAE framework to other models and scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) aim to disentangle model activations into monosemantic, human-interpretable features. In practice, learned features are often redundant and vary across training runs and sparsity levels, which makes interpretations difficult to transfer and reuse. We introduce Distilled Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders (DMSAEs), a training pipeline that distills a compact core of consistently useful features and reuses it to train new SAEs. DMSAEs run an iterative distillation cycle: train a Matryoshka SAE with a shared core, use gradient X activation to measure each feature's contribution to next-token loss in the most nested reconstruction, and keep only the smallest subset that explains a fixed fraction of the attribution. Only the core encoder weight vectors are transferred across cycles; the core decoder and all non-core latents are reinitialized each time. On Gemma-2-2B layer 12 residual stream activations, seven cycles of distillation (500M tokens, 65k width) yielded a distilled core of 197 features that were repeatedly selected. Training using this distilled core improves several SAEBench metrics and demonstrates that consistent sets of latent features can be transferred across sparsity levels

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Encode Scientific Quality? An Empirical Study Using Monosemantic Features from Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concept of scientific quality using monosemantic features extracted from sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first systematic investigation into how LLMs encode scientific quality using monosemantic features from sparse autoencoders, identifying four key types of features related to research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode a rich and multidimensional representation of scientific quality through monosemantic features, capturing aspects like research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon, providing insights into their internal mechanisms for research evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode features reflecting research methodologies, associating higher quality with rigorous methodological approaches.
Features related to publication type, such as survey papers and literature reviews, are associated with higher scholarly impact.
Features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies act as strong signals of perceived research importance.
Features corresponding to specific scientific jargons and academic language are identified, though their precise role is unclear.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of monosemantic features inherently involves a qualitative component, as semantic labels are assigned by human researchers and may introduce subjectivity.
This work focused exclusively on Gemma 2 models, limiting the generality of the results to other architectures.
The study classified publications into research quality quartiles rather than using regression to predict specific values.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other LLM architectures to assess the generality of the results.
Using regression to predict specific quality values instead of classification into quartiles.
Investigating how interpretable features can enhance LLM performance in tasks such as research evaluation, academic text generation, and hypothesis discovery.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing use of generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) in particular, to support both the assessment and generation of scientific work. Although some studies have shown that LLMs can, to a certain extent, evaluate research according to perceived quality, our understanding of the internal mechanisms that enable this capability remains limited. This paper presents the first study that investigates how LLMs encode the concept of scientific quality through relevant monosemantic features extracted using sparse autoencoders. We derive such features under different experimental settings and assess their ability to serve as predictors across three tasks related to research quality: predicting citation count, journal SJR, and journal h-index. The results indicate that LLMs encode features associated with multiple dimensions of scientific quality. In particular, we identify four recurring types of features that capture key aspects of how research quality is represented: 1) features reflecting research methodologies; 2) features related to publication type, with literature reviews typically exhibiting higher impact; 3) features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies; and 4) features corresponding to specific scientific jargons. These findings represent an important step toward understanding how LLMs encapsulate concepts related to research quality.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: k-Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How effective is sparsity by itself as a regularizer and nonlinearity in autoencoders for feature learning and classification?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the k-sparse autoencoder, a fast sparse coding method that enforces exact sparsity in hidden units, and shows it achieves better classification results than denoising autoencoders, dropout, and RBMs on MNIST and NORB.
papers.conclusion: The k-sparse autoencoder is a fast and effective sparse coding method that achieves state-of-the-art classification results by enforcing sparsity alone, without other nonlinearities or penalties.
papers.key_findings:
The k-sparse autoencoder achieves better classification performance than denoising autoencoders, dropout autoencoders, and RBMs on MNIST and NORB datasets.
The sparsity level k controls the locality of learned features; higher k yields more local features, lower k yields more global features.
The method is simple to train and fast for encoding, making it suitable for large problem sizes.
k-sparse autoencoders can be used for pre-training shallow and deep discriminative neural networks, achieving results comparable to state-of-the-art.
A scheduling strategy for the sparsity level during training helps avoid dead hidden units and improves training.
papers.limitation: Too low sparsity level (k) can lead to dead hidden units and features that are too global, not factoring the input into parts.
papers.abstract: Recently, it has been observed that when representations are learnt in a way that encourages sparsity, improved performance is obtained on classification tasks. These methods involve combinations of activation functions, sampling steps and different kinds of penalties. To investigate the effectiveness of sparsity by itself, we propose the k-sparse autoencoder, which is an autoencoder with linear activation function, where in hidden layers only the k highest activities are kept. When applied to the MNIST and NORB datasets, we find that this method achieves better classification results than denoising autoencoders, networks trained with dropout, and RBMs. k-sparse autoencoders are simple to train and the encoding stage is very fast, making them well-suited to large problem sizes, where conventional sparse coding algorithms cannot be applied.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: CytoSAE: Interpretable Cell Embeddings for Hematology
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied for interpretable morphological concept discovery in hematological imaging?
papers.core_contribution: CytoSAE is a sparse autoencoder that discovers interpretable morphological concepts in hematological images, generalizes across diverse and out-of-domain datasets, and enables explainable disease classification at patch, image, patient, and disease levels.
papers.conclusion: CytoSAE successfully learns interpretable morphological features across different hematological datasets, maintains generalizability to out-of-domain data, and enables multi-level analysis for interpretable disease classification.
papers.key_findings:
CytoSAE discovers morphologically relevant concepts that generalize across peripheral blood and bone marrow cytology datasets, validated by medical experts.
Patch-wise attribution allows sub-cellular level analysis of concepts, highlighting consistent morphological features across datasets.
Patient-level concept barcodes reveal disease-specific morphological features for AML subtypes, such as monocytic precursors for CBFB::MYH11 and granulated blasts for PML::RARA.
CytoSAE concepts achieve multi-class classification performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning methods while providing explainability.
Ablation studies show the number of discovered concepts is stable across expansion factors and hyperparameters, with optimal layers between 7–11 for concept balance.
papers.limitation: Manual expert validation was conducted only at the dataset level, not per patient, to avoid human selection bias in concept discovery.
future_direction: Explore patient-specific concept retrieval while minimizing subjectivity.
Incorporate semi-supervised learning techniques to refine the discovered features further.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerged as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based foundation models. Very recently, SAEs were also adopted for the visual domain, enabling the discovery of visual concepts and their patch-wise attribution to tokens in the transformer model. While a growing number of foundation models emerged for medical imaging, tools for explaining their inferences are still lacking. In this work, we show the applicability of SAEs for hematology. We propose CytoSAE, a sparse autoencoder which is trained on over 40,000 peripheral blood single-cell images. CytoSAE generalizes to diverse and out-of-domain datasets, including bone marrow cytology, where it identifies morphologically relevant concepts which we validated with medical experts. Furthermore, we demonstrate scenarios in which CytoSAE can generate patient-specific and disease-specific concepts, enabling the detection of pathognomonic cells and localized cellular abnormalities at the patch level. We quantified the effect of concepts on a patient-level AML subtype classification task and show that CytoSAE concepts reach performance comparable to the state-of-the-art, while offering explainability on the sub-cellular level. Source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/dynamical-inference/cytosae.

papers.title: Sparse Semantic Dimension as a Generalization Certificate for LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) generalize robustly despite having parameter counts that vastly exceed the number of training tokens? The paper investigates whether the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the low-dimensional, sparse geometry of the model's internal representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that the effective complexity of LLMs is governed by the sparse, low-dimensional manifold of internal representations, and introduces the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) to provide non-vacuous generalization bounds that scale with the active feature pool rather than the parameter count.
papers.conclusion: The Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) resolves the generalization paradox by shifting the complexity measure from parameter count to the active feature pool, providing a mathematical certificate for generalization and a safety monitor for OOD detection via feature density.
papers.key_findings:
The SSD-based generalization bound becomes non-vacuous at realistic sample sizes (e.g., N≈50,000) for GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, where parameter-counting bounds would be vacuous.
Larger models (Gemma-2B) require significantly fewer calibration samples to identify their active manifold than smaller models (GPT-2), suggesting they learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs trigger a measurable 'feature explosion' (a sharp spike in active features), which serves as a reliable, computationally cheap proxy for epistemic uncertainty and can function as a safety monitor.
The generalization guarantee depends on the specific semantic alignment of activated SAE features, not just statistical sparsity, as shown by an ablation where shuffling feature indices causes a catastrophic increase in reconstruction error.
The framework decomposes generalization into interpretable components: empirical risk, reconstruction error, pool mismatch, and a complexity penalty based on the active concept pool size.
future_direction: Investigate how the ratio of SSD to parameter count evolves for frontier-scale models (e.g., 70B+ parameters) and whether a 'sparsity saturation' point exists.
Investigate layer-wise generalization dynamics by using SAEs at different layers to determine which layers govern memorization versus generalization.
Extend the theoretical bounds to account for dynamic or context-dependent concept pools to provide tighter guarantees for models operating in rapidly shifting domains.
papers.abstract: Standard statistical learning theory predicts that Large Language Models (LLMs) should overfit because their parameter counts vastly exceed the number of training tokens. Yet, in practice, they generalize robustly. We propose that the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the geometry of the model's internal representations: while the parameter space is high-dimensional, the activation states lie on a low-dimensional, sparse manifold. To formalize this, we introduce the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD), a complexity measure derived from the active feature vocabulary of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on the model's layers. Treating the LLM and SAE as frozen oracles, we utilize this framework to attribute the model's generalization capabilities to the sparsity of the dictionary rather than the total parameter count. Empirically, we validate this framework on GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, demonstrating that our bound provides non-vacuous certificates at realistic sample sizes. Crucially, we uncover a counter-intuitive "feature sharpness" scaling law: despite being an order of magnitude larger, Gemma-2B requires significantly fewer calibration samples to identify its active manifold compared to GPT-2, suggesting that larger models learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures. Finally, we show that this framework functions as a reliable safety monitor: out-of-distribution inputs trigger a measurable "feature explosion" (a sharp spike in active features), effectively signaling epistemic uncertainty through learned feature violation. Code is available at: https://github.com/newcodevelop/sparse-semantic-dimension.

papers.title: Denoising Concept Vectors with Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of linear concept vectors for language model steering by denoising hidden representations using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SDCV, a method that uses sparse autoencoders to denoise hidden representations by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples, leading to improved steering success rates.
papers.conclusion: SDCV effectively mitigates noise in concept vectors and enhances steering performance, demonstrating that denoising representations is a promising direction for robust concept steering.
papers.key_findings:
SDCV improves steering success rates by 4-16% across six challenging concepts while maintaining topic relevance.
SDCV-enhanced difference-in-mean generally outperforms SDCV-enhanced linear probing.
The method is effective across different models (Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B).
Optimal values for top-k and scale factor are not linearly related to peak performance, likely due to superposition and SAE training objectives.
Counterfactual experiments show that amplifying non-top-k latents (noise) generally decreases steering success.
papers.limitation:
The approach is confined to model families for which SAEs have already been trained.
SAEs imperfectly disentangle features and struggle to accurately capture feature importance.
Optimal values for steering strength, k, and scale factor must be determined empirically, which is computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: Linear concept vectors effectively steer LLMs, but existing methods suffer from noisy features in diverse datasets that undermine steering robustness. We propose Sparse Autoencoder-Denoised Concept Vectors (SDCV), which selectively keep the most discriminative SAE latents while reconstructing hidden representations. Our key insight is that concept-relevant signals can be explicitly separated from dataset noise by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples. Applied to linear probing and difference-in-mean, SDCV consistently improves steering success rates by 4-16\% across six challenging concepts, while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to automatically generate and evaluate natural language interpretations for millions of features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated pipeline and five new scoring techniques (detection, fuzzing, surprisal, embedding, intervention) for generating and evaluating natural language interpretations of SAE features, which are more efficient than existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an automated pipeline for interpreting SAE features, introduces efficient scoring methods, and shows that intervention scoring can explain features not captured by correlational methods.
papers.key_findings:
New scoring methods (detection, fuzzing, surprisal, embedding, intervention) are more compute-efficient than simulation scoring and correlate with human judgments.
Intervention scoring provides causal explanations for features that are poorly explained by correlational methods.
Sampling activating contexts from the entire activation distribution improves interpretation quality compared to only top activations.
Larger explainer models produce better interpretations, but benefits saturate beyond a certain size.
SAE features are more interpretable than the original model's neurons.
papers.limitation:
The pipeline does not handle long-range features that activate over longer contexts.
Intervention scoring requires careful control of intervention strength to avoid trivial interpretability.
Existing scoring techniques have pitfalls, such as simulation scoring ignoring non-activating contexts.
future_direction: Explanation of long-range features that activate over longer contexts.
papers.abstract: While the activations of neurons in deep neural networks usually do not have a simple human-understandable interpretation, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to transform these activations into a higher-dimensional latent space which may be more easily interpretable. However, these SAEs can have millions of distinct latent features, making it infeasible for humans to manually interpret each one. In this work, we build an open-source automated pipeline to generate and evaluate natural language explanations for SAE features using LLMs. We test our framework on SAEs of varying sizes, activation functions, and losses, trained on two different open-weight LLMs. We introduce five new techniques to score the quality of explanations that are cheaper to run than the previous state of the art. One of these techniques, intervention scoring, evaluates the interpretability of the effects of intervening on a feature, which we find explains features that are not recalled by existing methods. We propose guidelines for generating better explanations that remain valid for a broader set of activating contexts, and discuss pitfalls with existing scoring techniques. We use our explanations to measure the semantic similarity of independently trained SAEs, and find that SAEs trained on nearby layers of the residual stream are highly similar. Our large-scale analysis confirms that SAE latents are indeed much more interpretable than neurons, even when neurons are sparsified using top-$k$ postprocessing. Our code is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/sae-auto-interp, and our explanations are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/EleutherAI/auto_interp_explanations.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Can LLMs Detect Their Confabulations? Estimating Reliability in Uncertainty-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How does in-context information influence model behavior and response uncertainty, and can uncertainty signals be used to predict response reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a context-controlled evaluation framework to study how context quality affects LLM responses, shows that token-level uncertainty can misalign with correctness under misleading context, and proposes a probing-based method using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation for improved reliability detection.
papers.conclusion: Providing accurate context improves model accuracy and confidence, while misleading context leads to confidently incorrect outputs, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. The probing-based approach using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation improves reliability detection over uncertainty-only baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Correct context improves both answer accuracy and model confidence.
Misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses.
Token-level uncertainty does not always align with correctness, particularly under misleading context.
Probing classifiers using aggregated hidden states from high-uncertainty tokens outperform direct uncertainty metrics for reliability detection.
Aggregating features from multiple tokens yields better performance than single-token features.
future_direction: Developing reliability-aware generation and context validation/filtering mechanisms for multi-turn or retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating fluent but incorrect content, known as confabulation, which poses increasing risks in multi-turn or agentic applications where outputs may be reused as context. In this work, we investigate how in-context information influences model behavior and whether LLMs can identify their unreliable responses. We propose a reliability estimation that leverages token-level uncertainty to guide the aggregation of internal model representations. Specifically, we compute aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from output logits to identify salient tokens and aggregate their hidden states into compact representations for response-level reliability prediction. Through controlled experiments on open QA benchmarks, we find that correct in-context information improves both answer accuracy and model confidence, while misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. Our probing-based method captures these shifts in model behavior and improves the detection of unreliable outputs across multiple open-source LLMs. These results underscore the limitations of direct uncertainty signals and highlight the potential of uncertainty-guided probing for reliability-aware generation.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance. Additionally, we propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a last-layer activation amplification module and a few LoRA layers, outperforming full LoRA fine-tuning on reasoning benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters. Our code and data are publicly released.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: Causal Interpretation of Sparse Autoencoder Features in Vision
papers.research_question: How to causally interpret sparse autoencoder features in vision transformers by identifying the image patches that drive activations, rather than relying on correlational activation maps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Causal Feature Explanation (CaFE), which uses effective receptive field attribution to provide causal explanations for SAE features in vision transformers, demonstrating improved faithfulness over activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: CaFE provides more faithful and semantically precise interpretations of visual features by using causal ERF-based explanations, preventing misinterpretation from activation-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
CaFE with ERF attribution more accurately identifies causal image patches for SAE feature activations compared to naive activation maps.
Non-localized SAE features exist, especially in higher layers, where activations scatter across the image.
ERF maps reveal hidden context dependencies, such as features requiring co-occurrence of multiple objects.
Insertion tests show that CaFE with AttnLRP achieves higher causal recovery rates than activation-based baselines.
The frequency of non-local features increases with transformer layer depth, peaking in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Computing the ERF for each feature requires both forward and backward passes, which may be costly for very deep SAEs.
Manual annotation of non-local features is inherently subjective; devising scalable, automated criteria remains future work.
future_direction: Devising scalable, automated criteria for identifying non-local features
Extending CaFE with ERF-based attribution to text modalities
papers.abstract: Understanding what sparse auto-encoder (SAE) features in vision transformers truly represent is usually done by inspecting the patches where a feature's activation is highest. However, self-attention mixes information across the entire image, so an activated patch often co-occurs with-but does not cause-the feature's firing. We propose Causal Feature Explanation (CaFE), which leverages Effective Receptive Field (ERF). We consider each activation of an SAE feature to be a target and apply input-attribution methods to identify the image patches that causally drive that activation. Across CLIP-ViT features, ERF maps frequently diverge from naive activation maps, revealing hidden context dependencies (e.g., a "roaring face" feature that requires the co-occurrence of eyes and nose, rather than merely an open mouth). Patch insertion tests confirm that CaFE more effectively recovers or suppresses feature activations than activation-ranked patches. Our results show that CaFE yields more faithful and semantically precise explanations of vision-SAE features, highlighting the risk of misinterpretation when relying solely on activation location.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
Intervening on these temporal difference features (lesioning or clamping) impairs performance and reduces correlations, demonstrating their causal involvement.
In a grid world task, Llama uses temporal difference-like features to predict the actions of a Q-learning agent.
In a graph learning task, Llama learns global graph structure similarly to the successor representation, and temporal difference features support this learning.
papers.limitation:
The sparse autoencoders are task-specific and not suitable for identifying reinforcement learning variables for arbitrary tasks.
A circuit-level understanding of how these representations come about remains unclear.
The alignment between the model's behavior and the Q-learning agent is not perfect.
future_direction: Build more generic sparse autoencoders for arbitrary tasks.
Replicate findings with different large language models.
Achieve a circuit-level understanding of how temporal difference representations are computed.
Extend the Q-learning model to account for repetition tendencies.
papers.abstract: In-context learning, the ability to adapt based on a few examples in the input prompt, is a ubiquitous feature of large language models (LLMs). However, as LLMs' in-context learning abilities continue to improve, understanding this phenomenon mechanistically becomes increasingly important. In particular, it is not well-understood how LLMs learn to solve specific classes of problems, such as reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in-context. Through three different tasks, we first show that Llama $3$ $70$B can solve simple RL problems in-context. We then analyze the residual stream of Llama using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and find representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token. We verify that these representations are indeed causally involved in the computation of TD errors and $Q$-values by performing carefully designed interventions on them. Taken together, our work establishes a methodology for studying and manipulating in-context learning with SAEs, paving the way for a more mechanistic understanding.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
papers.research_question: Can linear features (e.g., from Sparse Autoencoders, probes, and steering vectors) be transferred between language models of different sizes using affine mappings (model stitching), and what are the implications for efficiency and feature universality?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that affine mappings (stitches) between residual streams can effectively transfer linear features across language models, enabling compute-efficient training of Sparse Autoencoders and transfer of probes and steering vectors, while revealing differences in how semantic and structural features transfer.
papers.conclusion: Linear features can be transferred between language models via affine mappings, supporting weak universality and providing a method to improve the training efficiency of interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Using transferred SAEs as initialization can reduce FLOPs by ~50% when training SAEs on larger models.
Probes and steering vectors can be transferred between models with no additional training in specific cases (e.g., language steering).
Structural features (syntactic) transfer more consistently than semantic features, which are more polarized in transferability.
Specific functional features (e.g., entropy and attention deactivation features) preserve their roles after transfer.
Linear stitches support a weak universality hypothesis, showing that small and large models learn similar representation spaces.
papers.limitation:
Stitches are only trained on general internet text between models in the same family with the same tokenizer.
The scaling law analysis is theoretically incomplete due to lack of high-compute regime data to fit the irreducible loss.
The semantic/structural classification is imperfect and noisy due to reliance on another LLM for augmentations.
Probing and steering experiments are limited to particular tasks and settings.
future_direction: Verify findings in cross-family model settings and finetune stitches on special tokens or chat-templated data.
Explore other applications of stitches, such as transferring linear weight updates like LoRAs.
Expand probing and steering experiments to examine robustness and broader task settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that affine mappings between residual streams of language models is a cheap way to effectively transfer represented features between models. We apply this technique to transfer the weights of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) between models of different sizes to compare their representations. We find that small and large models learn similar representation spaces, which motivates training expensive components like SAEs on a smaller model and transferring to a larger model at a FLOPs savings. In particular, using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization can lead to 50% cheaper training runs when training SAEs on larger models. Next, we show that transferred probes and steering vectors can effectively recover ground truth performance. Finally, we dive deeper into feature-level transferability, finding that semantic and structural features transfer noticeably differently while specific classes of functional features have their roles faithfully mapped. Overall, our findings illustrate similarities and differences in the linear representation spaces of small and large models and demonstrate a method for improving the training efficiency of SAEs.

papers.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders extract relatively monosemantic features that are more interpretable than neurons, with most features being human-understandable.
Features can be used to intervene on and steer transformer generation, such as activating specific features to produce corresponding text like base64 or Arabic script.
Features are universal across different models and autoencoder runs, more similar to each other than to neurons, suggesting they reflect underlying data properties.
Features split into families as autoencoder size increases, providing different resolutions of understanding the same model components.
Despite having only 512 neurons, the MLP layer can represent tens of thousands of features through superposition, as shown by scaling the autoencoder.
papers.abstract: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition? Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis. Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators: Model Recovery in Function Spaces
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be extended to operate in infinite-dimensional function spaces for concept learning, and what advantages do functional representations offer over standard SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs) that operate in function spaces, specifically SAE-FNOs, which improve concept learning stability, robustness, and generalization compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Functional representations in SAE-NOs extend sparse autoencoders from detectors of concept presence to models that capture the underlying structure of the data, highlighting parameterization as a central driver of interpretability and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-FNO successfully recovers ground-truth concepts in synthetic data and converges to zero dictionary recovery error.
SAE-FNO generalizes to unseen input resolutions, unlike SAE-CNN which fails beyond training resolution.
SAE-FNO learns concepts that are stable across different sparsity levels and exhibit diverse correlations, overcoming the orthogonality bias of SAE-MLP.
SAE-FNO achieves higher concept utilization efficiency, requiring fewer concepts to represent data, especially for larger domains.
Lifting accelerates concept recovery by acting as a preconditioner and improves optimization.
papers.abstract: We frame the problem of unifying representations in neural models as one of sparse model recovery and introduce a framework that extends sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to lifted spaces and infinite-dimensional function spaces, enabling mechanistic interpretability of large neural operators (NO). While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that neural networks converge to similar representations across architectures, the representational properties of neural operators remain underexplored despite their growing importance in scientific computing. We compare the inference and training dynamics of SAEs, lifted-SAE, and SAE neural operators. We highlight how lifting and operator modules introduce beneficial inductive biases, enabling faster recovery, improved recovery of smooth concepts, and robust inference across varying resolutions, a property unique to neural operators.

papers.title: Evaluating and Designing Sparse Autoencoders by Approximating Quasi-Orthogonality
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be evaluated and designed with a theoretical grounding for sparsity, avoiding the need to manually tune the hyperparameter k?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Approximate Feature Activation (AFA), a theoretical framework linking input embedding norms to sparse feature activation norms, and top-AFA, an activation function that adaptively selects the number of active features per input without tuning k.
papers.conclusion: The AFA framework addresses a core limitation in SAE design by providing a principled way to link input embeddings to feature activations, and top-AFA SAE demonstrates improved performance over fixed-sparsity methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed top-AFA SAE outperforms top-k and batch top-k SAEs in reconstruction performance on GPT-2 layers.
The εLBO metric provides a different evaluation perspective on SAE quality compared to mean squared error (MSE).
The AFA formulation provides a closed-form estimate of the ℓ2-norm of sparse activations with provable error bounds.
Pre-trained SAE decoders often fail to achieve the level of quasi-orthogonality permitted by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.
Top-AFA allows adaptive per-input sparsity, removing the need for a fixed sparsity hyperparameter k.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis is limited to the linear representation hypothesis; extending AFA to more general superposition settings remains an open question.
Top-AFA introduces a new hyperparameter λAFA and can result in high ℓ0 values.
future_direction: Extending AFA to more general superposition settings, such as when Φ(·) is a two-layer neural network or other SAE variants like Matryoshka SAEs.
A deeper investigation into the necessity of the loss coefficient λAFA.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used in mechanistic interpretability research for large language models; however, the state-of-the-art method of using $k$-sparse autoencoders lacks a theoretical grounding for selecting the hyperparameter $k$ that represents the number of nonzero activations, often denoted by $\ell_0$. In this paper, we reveal a theoretical link that the $\ell_2$-norm of the sparse feature vector can be approximated with the $\ell_2$-norm of the dense vector with a closed-form error, which allows sparse autoencoders to be trained without the need to manually determine $\ell_0$. Specifically, we validate two applications of our theoretical findings. First, we introduce a new methodology that can assess the feature activations of pre-trained SAEs by computing the theoretically expected value from the input embedding, which has been overlooked by existing SAE evaluation methods and loss functions. Second, we introduce a novel activation function, top-AFA, which builds upon our formulation of approximate feature activation (AFA). This function enables top-$k$ style activation without requiring a constant hyperparameter $k$ to be tuned, dynamically determining the number of activated features for each input. By training SAEs on three intermediate layers to reconstruct GPT2 hidden embeddings for over 80 million tokens from the OpenWebText dataset, we demonstrate the empirical merits of this approach and compare it with current state-of-the-art $k$-sparse autoencoders. Our code is available at: https://github.com/SewoongLee/top-afa-sae.
